title.en: The Purucaya: Seven Dead Incas Enthroned in Gold
title.zh: 普魯卡亞:七位先王坐擁金座

region.en: House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 31, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: He disinterred the bodies of the seven deceased Incas, from Manco Ccapac to Yahuar-huaccac, which were all in the House of the Sun, enriching them with masks, head-dresses called chuco, medals, bracelets, sceptres called yauri or champi, and other ornaments of gold. He then placed them, in the order of their seniority, on a bench with a back, richly adorned with gold, and ordered great festivals to be celebrated with representations of the lives of each Inca. These festivals, which are called purucaya, were continued for more than four months. Great and sumptuous sacrifices were made to each Inca at the conclusion of the representation of his acts and life. This gave them such authority that it made all strangers adore them and worship them as gods; these strangers, when they beheld such majesty, humbled themselves and put up their hands to worship or mucha. The corpses were held in great respect and veneration until the Spaniards came to this land of Peru.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提掘出七位先王的遺體——自曼科·卡帕克至亞瓦爾-瓦卡克——皆藏於太陽之屋。他為他們添置面具、「丘科」頭飾、徽章、鐲環、名為「亞烏里」或「昌皮」的權杖及諸般金飾,再按輩分次序,將他們安置在飾滿黃金的靠背長椅上;又下令舉行盛大節慶,搬演每位印加王的生平。這種節慶稱為「普魯卡亞」,歷時四個多月。每位先王的功業演畢,便為其獻上豐盛祭祀。此舉威儀赫赫,四方來客見之,無不折腰俯首、舉手行「穆恰」崇拜之禮,奉先王如神明。直至西班牙人到來,這些先王遺體始終備受尊崇。

sensitivity.note: The purucaya as state theatre of the ancestor cult; the living king staging his dead predecessors.

title.en: The Two-Headed Serpent Talisman: Chuqui Ylla, Guauqui of Pachacuti
title.zh: 雙頭蛇護符:帕查庫提的伴身神楚基·伊利亞

region.en: House of the Sun, Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科太陽之屋(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 31, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Besides these corpses, Pachacuti made two images of gold. He called one of them Viracocha Pachayachachi: it represented the creator, and was placed on the right of the image of the Sun. The other was called Chuqui ylla, representing lightning, placed on the left of the Sun. This image was most highly venerated by all. Inca Yupanqui adopted this idol for his guauqui, because he said that it had appeared and spoken in a desert place and had given him a serpent with two heads, to carry about with him always, saying that while he had it with him, nothing sinister could happen in his affairs. To these idols the Inca gave the use of lands, flocks, and servants, especially of certain women who lived in the same House of the Sun, in the manner of nuns.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提另鑄兩尊金像:一尊名「維拉科查·帕查亞查奇」,代表造物主,置於太陽神像之右;另一尊名「楚基·伊利亞」,代表閃電,置於太陽神像之左,受萬眾至高崇敬。印加·尤潘琪將這尊神像收為自己的「瓜烏基」(伴身兄弟神):因為據他所言,此像曾在荒野現身、開口說話,並賜他一條雙頭蛇,命他隨身攜帶——只要此蛇在身,諸事便不會遭逢兇險。印加王撥給這些神像田地、畜群與僕役,尤其是那些住在太陽之屋、如修女般的女子。

sensitivity.note: The lightning-god as personal oracle-brother; the two-headed serpent talisman links to the amaru imagery.

title.en: 'I Tread on My Enemies': The Order of the Inca Triumph

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 33, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The triumph was after this manner. The warriors marched in order, in their companies, dressed in the best manner possible, with songs and dances, and the captives, their eyes on the ground, dressed in long robes with many tassels. They entered by the streets of the city, which were very well adorned to receive them. They went on, enacting their battles and victories, on account of which they triumphed. On reaching the House of the Sun, the spoils and prisoners were thrown on the ground, and the Inca walked over them, trampling on them and saying: 'I tread on my enemies.' The prisoners were silent without raising their eyes. This order was used in all their triumphs.
summary.zh: 凱旋儀式如下:戰士按部伍列隊而行,盛裝奏樂,載歌載舞;俘虜則身披綴滿流蘇的長袍,垂首不敢仰視,隨隊入城。街道妝點一新,以迎王師;隊伍且行且演,重現征戰得勝之狀。行至太陽之屋,戰利品與俘虜被拋擲於地;印加王從其上走過,踏踐而行,口誦:「我腳踏我的仇敵。」俘虜默然,不敢舉目。凡凱旋,皆循此儀。

sensitivity.note: The triumph liturgy as ritual humiliation; repeated verbatim formula in Sarmiento's war narratives.

title.en: The Necromancer's Stone: Inca Rocca Slays Inca Urco in the River
title.zh: 巫師之石:印加·羅卡河畔誅烏爾庫

region.en: Yucay valley and rock of Chupellusca (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 尤卡伊河谷與丘佩盧斯卡岩(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 33, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: Pachacuti heard that his brother Urco was in a valley called Yucay, four leagues from Cuzco, and that he had assembled some people. Fearing that the movement was intended against him the Inca marched there with his army. His brother Inca Rocca went with him, who had the reputation of being a great necromancer. Arriving at a place called Paca in the said valley, the Inca went out against his brother Urco, and there was a battle between them. Inca Rocca hurled a stone which hit Urco on the throat. The blow was so great that Urco fell into the river flowing down the ravine where they were fighting. Urco exerted himself and fled, swimming down the river, with his axe in his hand. In this way he reached a rock called Chupellusca, a league below Tampu, where his brothers overtook him and killed him. From thence the Inca Pachacuti Yupanqui, with his brother Inca Rocca, marched with their troops to Caquia Xaquixahuana to see his father, who refused ever to speak with or see him, owing to the rage he felt at the death of Inca Urco. But Inca Rocca went in where Viracocha was and said: 'Father! it is not reasonable that you should grieve so much at the death of Urco, for I killed him in self defence, he having come to kill me... Think no more of it, for my brother Pachacuti Yupanqui is to be Inca, and I hold that you should favour him and be as a father to him.' Seeing the resolution of his son Inca Rocca, Viracocha did not dare to reply or to contradict him. At the end of a short time Inca Viracocha died of grief at the death of Inca Urco, deprived and despoiled of all honour and property. They buried his body in Caquia Xaquixahuana.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提聞報:其兄烏爾庫在庫斯科四萊格外的尤卡伊谷糾集人馬,恐其意在圖己,便提兵征討。其兄印加·羅卡隨行——此人素有「大巫師」之名。行至谷中名為帕卡之地,印加王與烏爾庫接戰。印加·羅卡擲石擊中烏爾庫咽喉;一擊沉重,烏爾庫墜入溝壑間奔流的河水。他掙扎逃生,手持戰斧,順流泅泳而下,漂至坦普下游一萊格處的名為「丘佩盧斯卡」的岩石旁——兄弟們追至,將他殺死。帕查庫提·尤潘琪與印加·羅卡遂率兵赴夏基夏瓜納探望父親;老王因烏爾庫之死怒不可遏,拒不與長子言語相見。印加·羅卡入見維拉科查,說道:「父親!烏爾庫之死,何足如此哀慟?他是來殺我的,我自衛而誅之。您兒子眾多,不必為一人如此傷心。忘了吧——帕查庫提·尤潘琪當為印加王;依我之見,您應扶持他,如父待子。」印加·羅卡意志堅決,維拉科查不敢反駁,只好說:「就依你所言,凡事聽你安排。」不久之後,印加·維拉科查因烏爾庫之死憂傷而死,生前已被奪去一切榮銜財產。遺體葬於夏基夏瓜納。

sensitivity.note: Fratricide in the river; the necromancer epithet attaches to Inca Rocca in this tradition.

title.en: The Jar That Destroyed a Nation: The Potter of the Cuyos
title.zh: 一罐釀滅族之禍:庫約斯陶工擲器傷王

region.en: Cuyo-suyu, province of the Cuyos (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫約蘇尤庫約斯省(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 34, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: After this Inca Yupanqui took to wife a native of Choco named Mama Anahuarqui. For greater pleasure and enjoyment, away from business, he went to the town of the Cuyos, chief place of the province of Cuyo-suyu. Being one day at a great entertainment, a potter, servant of the Sinchi, without apparent reason, threw a stone or, as some say, one of the jars which they call ulti, at the Inca's head and wounded him. The delinquent, who was a stranger to the district, was seized and tortured to confess who had ordered him to do it. He stated that all the Sinchis of Cuyo-suyu, who were Cuyo Ccapac, Ayan-quilalama, and Apu Cunaraqui, had conspired to kill the Inca and rebel. This was false, for it had been extorted from fear of the torture, or, as some say, he said it because he belonged to a hostile tribe and wished to do them harm. But the Inca, having heard what the potter said, ordered all the Sinchis to be killed with great cruelty. After their deaths he slaughtered the people, leaving none alive except some children and old women. Thus was that nation destroyed, and its towns are desolate to this day.
summary.zh: 其後印加·尤潘琪娶喬科女子瑪瑪·阿納瓦爾基為后。為求逸樂、遠離政務,他前往庫約蘇尤省重鎮庫約斯鎮。一日大宴之上,辛奇家的一個陶工——外鄉人——無故向印加王擲出一塊石頭,或說擲出一只名為「烏爾蒂」的陶罐,擊傷其頭。兇手被擒,嚴刑拷打,逼問主使。他供稱:庫約蘇尤諸辛奇——庫約·卡帕克、阿揚-基拉拉馬、阿普·庫納拉基——曾密謀弒王作亂。此供實屬誣妄:或是刑求所迫,或是——如另一說——他本屬敵對部族,欲加害於人。然而印加王聞供大怒,命將諸辛奇盡數殘殺;隨後屠戮其民,僅留孩童與老婦。這一族便如此滅絕,其城邑至今荒蕪。

sensitivity.note: A thrown jar as the trigger of a massacre; Sarmiento flags the confession as extorted - preserved critically.

title.en: The Head in Llasa-huasi: The Fall of Chuchi Ccapac
title.zh: 利亞薩-瓦西中的首級:喬奇·卡帕克之敗亡

region.zh: 科利亞奧哈通-科利亞(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Inca tradition as given to Sarmiento de Gamboa, 1572; trans. Markham 1907

source.work: Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, History of the Incas, ch. 37, trans. Sir Clements Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1907

summary.en: The Sinchi of Collao was named Chuchi Ccapac or Colla Ccapac, who increased so much in power and wealth among the nations of Colla-suyu that he was respected by all the Collas, who called him Inca Ccapac. Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui determined to conquer him from a motive of jealousy. He sent a message to Chuchi Colla requesting him to serve and obey him or else to prepare for battle; Chuchi Colla replied proudly that he waited for the Inca to come and do homage to him, and that if the Inca did not choose to do so, he would prepare his head, with which he intended to drink in his triumph after the victory. In the battle, seeing that the Collas resisted so resolutely, Inca Yupanqui turned his face to his men saying in a loud voice: 'O Incas of Cuzco! conquerors of all the land! Are you not ashamed that people so inferior to you, and unequal in weapons, should be equal to you and resist for so long a time?' With this rebuke the troops pressed upon their enemies and broke them. Inca Yupanqui knew that the completion of the victory consisted in the capture of Chuchi Ccapac: seeing him in the midst of his people, the Inca attacked them at the head of his guards, took him prisoner. Chuchi Colla and the other Colla prisoners were placed before the Inca's litter dressed in long robes covered with tassels in derision; the captives and spoils were offered to the image of the Sun, and the Inca trod on all the spoils and captives. When the triumph was over, to give it a good finish, the Inca caused the head of Chuchi Ccapac to be cut off, and put in the house called Llasa-huasi with those of the other Sinchis he had killed. He caused the other Sinchis and captains of Chuchi Ccapac to be given to the wild beasts, kept shut up for the purpose, in a house called Samca-huasi - a prison for grave offences, into which serpents and toads were put with the delinquents.
summary.zh: 科利亞奧的辛奇名喬奇·卡帕克(亦稱科利亞-卡帕克),權勢財富日增,眾科利亞人尊之為「印加·卡帕克」。帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪心生妒忌,決意征討。先遣使命其臣服,否則一戰;喬奇·科利亞傲然答道:等印加王來向他朝貢;若不然,他將備好自己的頭顱——勝利之後,好拿來盛酒慶功!大戰之中,見科利亞人頑強抵抗,印加·尤潘琪回首大喝:「庫斯科的印加人!大地的征服者!難道不羞愧嗎?武器遜於你們的下等之民,竟能與你們相持如此之久!」軍心受激,猛攻破敵。印加王深知全勝在於生擒喬奇·卡帕克,遂親率衛隊直搗敵陣,將其擒獲。凱旋之日,喬奇·科利亞與眾俘身披綴滿流蘇的長袍,以示羞辱,排列於印加王轎前;俘虜與戰利品獻於太陽神像之前,印加王踏踐其上。慶功既畢,為收全功之效,印加王命斬喬奇·卡帕克之頭,與所誅諸辛奇之首一同貯於「利亞薩-瓦西」(量屋)之中;喬奇帳下諸辛奇與將領,則被投入「桑卡-瓦西」——重罪囚犯之獄,獄中飼養毒蛇與蟾蜍,以飼猛獸之名,行生吞之實。

sensitivity.note: The Colla defeat cycle known also from Salcamayhua; here the prison with serpents and toads is a named institution.

passages.text: This message caused much heaviness to Chuchi Colla, but he replied proudly that he waited for the Inca to come and do homage to him like the other nations that had been conquered by him, and that if the Inca did not choose to do so, he would prepare his head, with which he intended to drink in his triumph after the victory which he would win if they should come to a battle.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 37 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeing that the Collas resisted so resolutely, and stood so firmly in the battle, he turned his face to his men saying in a loud voice: 'O Incas of Cuzco! conquerors of all the land! Are you not ashamed that people so inferior to you, and unequal in weapons, should be equal to you and resist for so long a time?' With this he returned to the fight, and the troops, touched by this rebuke, pressed upon their enemies in such sort that they were broken and defeated.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 37 (Markham 1907); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the triumph was over, to give it a good finish, the Inca caused the head of Chuchi Ccapac to be cut off, and put in the house called Llasa-huasi, with those of the other Sinchis he had killed. He caused the other Sinchis and captains of Chuchi Ccapac to be given to the wild beasts, kept shut up for the purpose, in a house called Samca-huasi.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Sarmiento, History of the Incas, ch. 37 (Markham 1907); not verbatim; Markham's note glosses Samca-huasi as a prison where serpents and toads were put in with the delinquents.

texts.canonical_translation: Sir Clements Markham, History of the Incas (Hakluyt Society, 1907)
